title: The fourth sight: a wanderer
hook: a shaven man in a robe, owning nothing, calm
carry: there is another way to live

segments.voice: Yesterday: marana, death, a funeral on the road, and the prince going quiet. Your line: everyone we love will go. Today, the last of the four sights.

A shaved head. A plain robe the color of earth. A bowl, and as far as anyone can tell, nothing else. Three rides have brought three shocks: age, sickness, death. If the story stopped there, it would be a very sad one, and the prince might have hidden in his gardens for life. But on a fourth ride, more troubled than he has ever been, he sees this man walking along the road. And his face is calm. Not cheerful, not grim. Calm, in a world that just showed the prince three reasons to despair.
screen: `A SHAVED HEAD, A BOWL, A ROBE.` → `THREE RIDES, THREE SHOCKS.` → `A CALM FACE.`

segments.voice: Who is that, the prince asks. Channa says: a samana. A wanderer, one who has gone forth. The word comes from a root meaning to strive, to make an effort. The Buddha's India had many of them: men, and some women, who left home, gave up property and family life, and walked the roads seeking answers to exactly the prince's questions. Why do we age? Why do we suffer? Is there a way out? They lived on what people put in their bowls, slept in forests and caves, and debated each other in public halls. They weren't one group; there were many teachers and many paths. The Jains, whose tradition is still alive today, came from this same world. So did the Buddha: for the rest of his life, outsiders would call him the samana Gotama. Here's the heart of the fourth sight. The first three were questions. The fourth was a possibility. Age, sickness and death come for everyone, palace or no palace. And here was someone who had looked at the same facts and was not afraid. The stories say something in the prince went still and bright. Not an answer yet. Just the sense that there is another way to live, and someone is already living it. That's where his search begins.
screen: `SAMANA — ONE WHO STRIVES.` · `MANY WANDERERS, MANY PATHS.` · `THREE QUESTIONS, ONE POSSIBILITY.` · `SOMEONE ALREADY LIVES IT.` · then, large: `THERE IS ANOTHER WAY TO LIVE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the calmest face you have ever seen: a teacher, a grandparent, a stranger on a train, even a statue. Notice the eyes, the mouth, the shoulders. Then let your own face do a little of the same: soften the jaw, rest the eyes, and let calm be possible for a minute.
Samana. A wanderer, one who strives: someone who has left home to seek the truth. The fourth sight, and the first hope.
Your line: there is another way to live. Calm, it turns out, is possible. Four sights, all seen.

howItsDone: Buddhist monks and nuns today still follow the samana's way of life in many places, shaving their heads, wearing robes and receiving food as alms, and lay Buddhists often honor them as living examples of another way to live.

original.note: Pali: a wanderer, an ascetic, one who strives. Sanskrit śramaṇa.

trapdoor: what you thought: a monk the prince happened to see.
what it means: after three sights of suffering, the fourth shows someone at peace with the same facts. it's the first hope in the story.
what a scholar hears: samana (Sanskrit śramaṇa), from a root meaning to exert oneself; the samana movements, including Jains and Ajivikas, stood outside the brahmin priesthood.
recall: the Buddha's name: one whose aim succeeds

chat.says: After three sad sights, what was so special about the fourth one?
options: A calm wanderer showed him another way to live was possible.
A doctor told him age and sickness could one day be cured.
A king showed him how to rule a kingdom without fear.
chat.meaning: The first three sights were questions. The calm samana was a possibility: someone facing the same facts without fear.

samana.meaning: a wanderer who has left home to seek the truth

Jains.meaning: followers of Jainism, an Indian path still alive today

Channa.meaning: the prince's charioteer, who answered him plainly

sources.ref: Mahapadana Sutta (Digha Nikaya 14): the one gone forth, the fourth sight

notes: Etymology of samana/śramaṇa from the root śram, to exert oneself; confirm.
'Some women' among the wanderers: women ascetics (e.g., among the Jains) are attested; confirm the phrasing is fair for the period.
'The samana Gotama' as outsiders' name for the Buddha: common in the suttas (samano Gotamo). Confirm.
The prince's inner response to the fourth sight is from the later biographies; DN 14 has Vipassi decide to go forth. Confirm the framing.
